hook: Clocks fall back today, but time zones were invented by railroads, not government.
beats: Before 1883, every town set its clocks by the sun, so noon changed from town to town.
On November 18, 1883, US and Canadian railroads reset their clocks to four zones, making a Day of Two Noons.
Congress only made standard time zones official law in 1918, thirty-five years later.
question: Would you keep the clock change or end it?
title: Railroads Invented Your Time Zone, Not the Government
source: Library of Congress, 'The Day of Two Noons' (Business History research guide)

hook: Those Leonid shooting stars are mostly grains of sand, not rocks.
beats: The Leonids come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle, which sheds dust along its orbit every 33 years.
Those tiny grains hit our atmosphere at about 44 miles per second, fastest of any major shower.
At that speed, the air in front of each grain superheats and glows, making the bright streak.
question: Have you ever seen a shooting star?
title: Shooting Stars Are Mostly Specks of Sand

trend: Perseverance rover sets Mars driving record
hook: Perseverance just drove a record 28 miles on Mars, where sunsets are blue.
beats: On Earth, air scatters blue light away, so our sunsets look red and orange.
Mars is the opposite: its sky is full of fine dust that behaves differently.
The dust turns the daytime sky butterscotch, but the glow around the setting sun looks blue.
question: Would you watch a Mars sunset?
title: Sunsets on Mars Are Blue, Not Red
source: NASA Science (Mars Exploration Program, rover sunset images)

hook: Voyager 1 is so far away that a message takes a full day.
beats: On November 18, the probe will be 16.1 billion miles away, one full light-day.
Radio signals travel at light speed, so a command takes 24 hours to arrive.
Its reply takes another day. After 49 years, it has covered just 0.0027% of the way to Proxima Centauri.
question: Would you wait 2 days for a text reply?
title: Voyager 1 Is So Far, Messages Take a Whole Day
source: NASA Science (Night Sky Notes) and NASA JPL Voyager mission

hook: Tonight's Taurid fireballs come from a comet that circles the Sun every 3.3 years.
beats: That comet is Encke, and NASA lists its 3.3-year orbit as the shortest of any known comet.
Each trip near the Sun, its ice warms up and sheds dust and gravel along its path.
Every autumn, Earth crosses that trail, and bits hit our air at about 17 miles per second.
